newsitem.title: MEXICO: Disorganization mutes Mexico Indian cry for justice.
newsitem.headline: Disorganization mutes Mexico Indian cry for justice.

text.p: Indians from across Mexico tried to denounce injustice at a national congress on Wednesday, but the absence of the star guests, the Zapatista rebels, left them floundering in a morass of organisational bureaucracy.

The National Indigenous Congress was billed as a unique chance for 450 representatives from more than 40 ethnic groups to press demands for land rights, better education and health and an end to poverty.
The event caught national headlines after Zapatista Indian rebels in southern Mexico announced they planned to defy the government and make a first trip to the capital to attend.

But after the first full session drew to a close with no Zapatistas in sight, delegates in the half-empty main hall had decided only agenda points and those trying to denounce specific injustices were silenced by an officious chair.

"We can't stand Mexico being handed over to foreigners any longer," said Amalia Salas, a brightly dressed Indian from the Xochimilco district in southern Mexico City. "We need help -- all our land is being delivered to foreigners."
As she collapsed in tears over the microphone, a stern riposte came from the chair, saying the discussion should be limited to deciding the conference agenda.

Banners pinned to the walls of the National Medical Centre congress hall where the event was being held gave the flavor of the laborious discussions. "Pluri-ethnic autonomous regions of Chiapas present," read one.

The 1994 Zapatista rebellion in Chiapas put Mexico's long-neglected Indians into the spotlight, but also led to a bewildering proliferation of regional Indian forums, discussion groups, Internet pages and communiques, of which Wednesday's National Congress was the latest.
Outside, a "civil cordon for peace" -- a bunch of youths in jeans and white T-shirts holding a white cord -- said they were guarding participants against unknown "agents provocateurs."

Vendors peddled Che Guevara mementos, Indian handicrafts and a hammer and sickle Soviet flag, while a loudspeaker blared criticism of the "mercantilist Pope who sold the Mexican people out to the most recalcitrant reactionary financial groups."
